newsitem.title: USA: Gold Institute sees gold output rise through 1999.
newsitem.headline: Gold Institute sees gold output rise through 1999.

text.p: World gold mine production is expected to increase steadily over the next three years reaching 83.1 million ounces by 1998, and remain at that level in 1999, according to the Gold Institute's latest forecasts.
South African gold production has dropped steadily in the past decade and is projected to fall another 13 percent by 1999, the Washington DC based Gold Institute said.
South African output in 1995 totalled 16.8 million ounces and is forecast to fall to 14.6 million ounces by 1999.

As the world's second largest gold producer, the U.S. now produces about 15 percent of world gold supplies and expects continued increases to 1998 at 13.9 million ounces, with a slight decline seen in 1999 to 12.7 million ounces.

"Although major reform of the nation's mining law has not yet occurred, the uncertainty it creates, in addition to the time consuming permission process - now averaging almost five years - has led many gold mining companies to reduce investment in exploration and mine development here which will have an impact on future U.S. production," the report said.
Australia is seen replacing the U.S. as the world's second largest gold producer in the next four years, the report said.
Although Australian production fell slightly in 1995, mine supply is forecast to grow a significant 38 percent by 1999 reaching 11.2 million ounces.

In addition to technological advances in production, Australia's projected increases are also seen dependent on hedging strategies which have brought producers greater certainty in cash flows, the report said.

CIS (former Soviet Union) production, which fell by 9.3 percent in 1995, is seen falling further to seven million ounces in 1996, before increasing to 7.2 million ounces in 1997 and 7.5 million in 1998 and 1999.
Canada, the world's fifth largest producer, is projecting a 21 percent increase over the next four years, reaching 5.7 million ounces by 1999.
The forecasts were compiled by the Gold Institute, with contributions from more than 100 mining groups from 70 countries.
The Gold Institute is an international association representing miners, refiners, and wholesalers of gold products.
